key_insight: This paper frames embodiment as an active control problem: intelligent agents should monitor internal states, not just external rewards, and adapt behavior to maintain functional balance. It connects cybernetics, interoception, reinforcement learning, and neuroscience into a unified view of autonomous decision-making.
problem_solved: It addresses the gap in AI systems that react to the environment but do not explicitly model their own internal condition, limits, or needs. The work aims to improve autonomy and robustness by giving agents a mechanism similar to biological interoception.
method: Builds a cybernetic framework inspired by how organisms regulate internal physiological states.
Integrates interoceptive signals with reinforcement learning so actions are guided by both external and internal feedback.
Draws on neuroscience concepts of embodiment to inform agent design and adaptive control.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a path toward more resilient, self-regulating agents that can adapt to changing conditions without relying only on reward maximization. It is especially relevant for embodied AI, robotics, and long-horizon autonomous systems.
visual_elements: A feedback-loop diagram showing environment, agent, and internal state regulation.
A side-by-side comparison of standard RL vs interoception-aware RL.
An embodiment schematic with sensors, internal variables, policy, and action outputs.
Simple icons for physiology, control, adaptation, and learning.
paper_title: Cybernetics, interoception, and the art of embodiment
